title: Your First 60 Days After Inheriting a Bigger Team
author: Ethan Evans
summary: Ethan Evans provides a practical 60-day framework for leaders who have just inherited a larger team through promotion, reorganization, or acquisition — a scenario where people, context, and expectations all change simultaneously. The article argues that the first 60 days are not for proving yourself through bold moves or immediate results but for building the relational and informational foundation without which any action will be premature and likely counterproductive. Evans outlines a structured listening phase: individual conversations with every team member to understand their work, concerns, and view of what the team needs. A diagnostic phase follows — identifying the team's genuine strengths, the critical risks, and the single most important bottleneck — before any visible structural changes. The article warns against the most common failure mode: moving too quickly on organizational changes before earning the right to make them or understanding what the existing culture does well. Evans closes with the principle that in the first 60 days, being respected matters more than being liked, and being informed matters more than being decisive.
points: The first 60 days are a listening and learning investment, not a performance period; leaders who make early structural moves before completing relational and informational groundwork almost always have to undo those moves at significant cost to team trust.

Individual conversations with every team member in the first two weeks are non-negotiable — they are the primary data-collection mechanism and the first demonstration that the new leader sees people as individuals rather than organizational units.

The diagnostic phase should answer three questions: what is this team genuinely excellent at, what is the single most critical risk right now, and what is the one bottleneck limiting everything else — three answers that structure every subsequent decision.

Inherited teams have developed cultural adaptations to their previous leader that may look like dysfunction but actually serve important purposes; understanding those adaptations before changing them is the mark of organizational intelligence.

Being respected (earned through attentiveness, follow-through, and fairness) matters more than being liked in the first 60 days — relationships built on respect are more durable and more useful for navigating hard decisions than relationships built on approval.
